{{Short description|Integral in integration theory}}
In the branch of [[mathematics]] known as [[Integral|integration theory]], the '''McShane integral''', created by [[Edward J. McShane]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McShane |first=E. J. |date=1973 |title=A Unified Theory of Integration |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2319078 |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=80 |issue=4 |pages=349–359 |doi=10.2307/2319078 |jstor=2319078 |issn=0002-9890|url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a modification of the [[Henstock–Kurzweil integral|Henstock-Kurzweil integral]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Kurtz |first=Douglas S. and Swartz, Charles W. |title=Theories of integration: the integrals of Riemann, Lebesgue, Henstock-Kurzweil, and McShane |date=2012 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-4368-99-5 |edition=2nd |location=Singapore |pages=247 |oclc=769192118}}</ref> The McShane integral is equivalent to the [[Lebesgue integral]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Gordon |first=Russell A. |title=The integrals of Lebesgue, Denjoy, Perron, and Henstock |date=1994 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=0-8218-3805-9 |location=Providence, R.I. |pages=157–163 |oclc=30474120}}</ref>

== Definition ==

=== Free tagged partition ===
Given a closed interval {{closed-closed|''a'', ''b''}} of the [[Number line|real line]], a ''free tagged partition'' <math>P</math> ''of'' <math>[a,b]</math> is a set

: <math>\{(t_i, [a_{i-1}, a_i]) : 1 \leq i \leq n  \} </math>

where

: <math> a = a_0 < a_1 < \dots < a_n = b </math>

and each tag <math> t_i \in [a, b]</math>.

The fact that the tags are allowed to be outside the subintervals is why the partition is called ''free''. It's also the only difference between the definitions of the Henstock-Kurzweil integral and the McShane integral.

For a function <math>f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}</math> and a free tagged partition <math>P</math>, define <math>S(f, P) = \sum_{i = 1}^n f(t_i) (a_i - a_{i-1}).</math>

=== Gauge ===
A positive function <math> \delta : [a, b] \to (0, +\infty) </math> is called a ''gauge'' in this context.

We say that a free tagged partition <math>P</math> is <math>\delta</math>''-fine'' if for all <math>i = 1,2, \dots, n,</math>

: <math>[a_{i-1}, a_i] \subseteq [t_i - \delta(t_i), t_i + \delta(t_i)]. </math>

Intuitively, the gauge controls the widths of the subintervals. Like with the [[Henstock–Kurzweil integral|Henstock-Kurzweil integral]], this provides flexibility (especially near problematic points) not given by the [[Riemann integral]].

=== McShane integral ===
The value <math>\int_a^b f</math> is the McShane integral of <math>f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}</math> if for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> we can find a gauge <math>\delta</math> such that for all <math>\delta</math>-fine free tagged partitions <math>P</math> of <math>[a,b]</math>,

: <math> \left |\int_a^bf - S(f, P) \right| < \varepsilon. </math>

== Examples ==
It's clear that if a function <math>f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}</math> is integrable according to the McShane definition, then <math>f</math> is also Henstock-Kurzweil integrable. Both integrals coincide in the regard of its uniqueness. 

In order to illustrate the above definition we analyse the McShane integrability of the functions described in the following examples, which are already known as Henstock-Kurzweil integrable (see the paragraph 3 of the site of this Wikipedia "[[Henstock-Kurzweil integral]]"). 

=== Example 1 ===
Let <math>f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}</math> be such that <math>f(a)=f(b)=0</math> and <math display="inline">f(x)=1</math> if <math display="inline">x\in]a,b[.</math>

As is well known, this function is Riemann integrable and the correspondent integral is equal to <math>b-a.</math> We will show that this <math>f</math> is also McShane integrable and that its integral assumes the same value.

For that purpose, for a given <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, let's choose the gauge <math>\delta(t)</math> such that <math>\delta(a)=\delta(b)=\varepsilon/4</math> and <math>\delta(t)=b-a</math> if <math display="inline">t\in]a,b[.</math>

Any free tagged partition <math>P=\{(t_i, [a_{i-1}, a_i]) : i=1,...,n\} </math> of <math>[a,b] </math> can be decomposed into sequences like

<math>(a,[x_{i_j-1},x_{i_j}])</math>, for <math>j=1,...,\lambda</math>,

<math>(b,[x_{i_k-1},x_{i_k}])</math>, for <math>k=1,...,\mu</math>, and

<math>(t_{i_r},[x_{i_r-1},x_{i_r}])</math>, where <math>r=1,...,\nu</math>, such that <math>t_{i_r}\in]a,b[</math> <math>(\lambda+\mu+\nu=n).</math>

This way, we have the Riemann sum

<math>S(f, P) = \sum_{r=1}^\nu \displaystyle(x_{i_r}-x_{i_r-1})</math>

and by consequence

<math>|S(P,f)-(b-a)|=\textstyle \sum_{j=1}^\lambda \displaystyle(x_{i_j}-x_{i_j-1})+\textstyle \sum_{k=1}^\mu \displaystyle(x_{i_k}-x_{i_k-1}).</math>

Therefore if <math>P</math> is a free tagged <math>\delta</math>-fine partition we have

<math>[x_{i_j-1},x_{i_j}]\subset[a-\delta(a),a+\delta(a)]</math>, for every <math>j=1,...,\lambda</math>, and

<math>[x_{i_k-1},x_{i_k}]\subset[b-\delta(b),b+\delta(b)]</math>, for every <math>k=1,...,\mu</math>.

Since each one of those intervals do not overlap the interior of all the remaining, we obtain

<math>|S(P,f)-(b-a)| <2\delta(a)+2\delta(b)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}=\varepsilon.</math>

Thus  <math>f</math> is McShane integrable and

<math>\int_a^b f=b-a.</math>

The next example proves the existence of a distinction between Riemann and McShane integrals.

=== Example 2 ===
Let <math>d:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> the well known Dirichlet's function given by

<math>d(x) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if }x\text{ is rational,} \\0, & \text{if }x\text{ is irrational,} \end{cases}</math>

which one knows to be not Riemann integrable. We will show that <math>d</math> is integrable in the McShane sense and that its integral is zero.

Denoting by <math>\{r_1,r_2,...,r_n,...\}</math> the set of all rational numbers of the interval <math>[a,b]</math>, for any <math>\varepsilon>0</math> let's formulate the following gauge

<math>\delta(x) = \begin{cases} \varepsilon2^{-n-1}, & \text{if }x=r_n\text{ and } n=1,2,...,\\1, & \text{if }x\text{ is irrational.} \end{cases}</math>

For any <math>\delta</math>-fine free tagged partition <math>P=\{(t_i,[x_{i-1},x_i]):i=1,...,n\}</math> consider its Riemann sum

<math>S(P,f)=\textstyle \sum_{i=1}^n \displaystyle f(t_i)(x_i-x_{i-1})</math>.

Taking into account that <math>f(t_i)=0</math> whenever <math>t_i</math> is irrational, we can exclude in the sequence of ordered pairs which constitute <math>P</math>, the pairs <math>(t_i,[x_{i-1},x_i])</math> where <math>t_i</math> is irrational. The remainder are subsequences of the type <math>(r_k,[x_{i_1-1},x_{i_1}]),...,(r_k,[x_{i_k-1},x_{i_k}])</math> such that <math>[x_{i_j-1},x_{i_j}]\subset [r_k-\delta(r_k),r_k+\delta(r_k)]</math>, <math>j=1,...,k.</math> Since each one of those intervals do not overlap the interior of the remaining, each one of these sequences gives rise in the [[Riemann sum]] to subsums of the type

<math display="inline">\textstyle \sum_{j=1}^k \displaystyle f(r_k)(x_{i_j}-x_{i_j-1})=\textstyle \sum_{j=1}^k \displaystyle (x_{i_j}-x_{i_j-1})\leq2\delta(r_k)=\frac{\varepsilon}{2^n}</math>.

Thus <math display="inline">0\leq S(P,f)<\textstyle \sum_{n\geq1} \displaystyle \varepsilon/2^n=\varepsilon</math>, which proves that the Dirichlet's function is McShane integrable and that

<math>\int_a^b d=0.</math>

== Relationship with Derivatives ==
For real functions defined on an interval <math>[a,b]</math>, both Henstock-Kurzweil and McShane integrals satisfy the elementary properties enumerated below, where by <math display="inline">\int_{a}^{b} f</math> we denote indistinctly the value of anyone of those integrals.

# If <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> then <math>f</math> is integrable on each subinterval of <math>[a,b]</math>.
# If <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,c]</math> and <math>[c,b]</math> then <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> and <math display="inline">\int_{a}^{c} f+\int_{c}^{b} f=\int_{a}^{b} f</math>.
# If <math>f</math> is continuous on <math>[a,b]</math> then <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math>.
# If <math>f</math> is monotonous on <math>[a,b]</math> then <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math>.
# Let <math>\phi:[a,b]\rightarrow[\alpha,\beta]</math> be a differentiable and strictly monotonous function. Then <math>f:[\alpha,\beta]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is integrable on <math>[\alpha,\beta]</math> [[if and only if]] <math display="inline">(f\circ\phi)|\phi'|</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math>. In such case <math display="inline">\int_{a}^{b} (f\circ\phi)|\phi'|=\int_{\alpha}^{\beta} f</math>.
# If <math>f</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> then <math>kf</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> and <math display="inline">\int_{a}^{b}kf=k\int_{a}^{b}f</math>, for every <math>k\in \mathbb{R}</math>.
# Let <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> be integrable on <math>[a,b]</math>. Then:
#* <math>f+g</math> is integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> and <math display="inline">\int_{a}^{b} (f+g)=\int_{a}^{b} f+\int_{a}^{b} g</math>.
#* <math>f\leq g </math> on <math>\left[ a,b\right]</math><math display="inline">\Rightarrow  \int_{a}^{b}f\leq \int_{a}^{b}g</math>.

With respect to the integrals mentioned above, the proofs of these properties are identical excepting slight variations inherent to the differences of the correspondent definitions (see Washek Pfeffer<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Pfeffer |first=Washek F. |title=The Riemann Approach to Integration |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1993 |isbn=0-521-44035-1 |location=New York}}</ref> [Sec. 6.1]).

This way a certain parallelism between the two integrals is observed. However an imperceptible rupture occurs when other properties are analysed, such as the absolute integrability and the integrability of the derivatives of integrable differentiable functions.

On this matter the following theorems hold (see<ref name=":0" /> [Prop.2.2.3 e Th. 6.1.2]).

=== Theorem 1 (on the absolute integrability of the McShane integral) ===
If <math>f:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is McShane integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> then <math>|f|</math> is also McShane integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> and<math display="inline">|\int_{a}^{b} f|\leq\int_{a}^{b} |f|</math>.

=== Theorem 2 (fundamental theorem of Henstock-Kurzweil integral) ===
If <math display="inline">F:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> is differentiable on <math>[a,b]</math>, then <math display="inline">F'</math> is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable on <math>[a,b]</math> and<math display="inline">\int_{a}^{b} F'=F(b)-F(a)</math>.

In order to illustrate these theorems we analyse the following example based upon Example 2.4.12.<ref name=":0" />

=== Example 3 ===
Let's consider the function:

<math>F(x) = \begin{cases} x^2\cos(\pi/x^2), & \text{if }x\neq0, \\ 0, & \text{if }x=0. \end{cases}</math>

<math>F</math> is obviously differentiable at any <math>x\neq0</math> and differentiable, as well, at  <math>x=0</math>, since <math display="inline">\lim_{x \to 0}\left ( \frac{F(x)}{x} \right )=\lim_{x \to 0}\left ( x\cos\frac{\pi}{x^2} \right )=0</math>.

Moreover

<math display="inline">F'(x) = \begin{cases} 2x\cos(\pi/x^2)+ \frac{2\pi}{x}\sin(\pi/x^2) , & \text{if }x\neq0, \\ 0, & \text{if }x=0. \end{cases}</math>

As the function

<math>h(x) = \begin{cases} 2x\cos(\pi/x^2), & \text{if }x\neq0, \\ 0, & \text{if }x=0, \end{cases}</math>

is continuous and, by the Theorem 2, the function <math>F'(x)</math> is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable on <math>[0,1],</math> then by the properties 6 and 7, the same holds to the function

<math display="inline">g_0(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x} \sin(\pi/x^2), & \text{if }x\neq0, \\ 0, & \text{if }x=0. \end{cases}</math>

But the function

<math display="inline">g(x)=|g_0(x) |= \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x} |\sin(\pi/x^2)|, & \text{if }x\neq0, \\ 0, & \text{if }x=0, \end{cases}</math>

is not integrable on <math>[0,1]</math> for none of the mentioned integrals.

In fact, otherwise, denoting by <math display="inline">\int_{0}^{1} g(x) dx</math> anyone of such integrals, we should have necessarily <math display="inline">\int_{0}^{1} g(x) dx\geq\int_{1/\sqrt{n}}^{1} \frac{1}{x} |\sin(\pi/x^2)| dx,</math> for any positive [[integer]] <math>n</math>. Then through the change of variable <math display="inline">x=1/\sqrt{t}</math>, we should obtain taking into account the property 5:

<math>\int_{1/\sqrt{n}}^{1} \frac{1}{x} |\sin(\pi/x^2)| dx=\frac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{n} \frac{1}{t} |\sin(\pi t)| dt
=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=2}^n\int_{k-1}^{k} \frac{1}{t} |\sin(\pi t)| dt\geq</math>

<math>\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=2}^n\frac{1}{k} \int_{k-1}^{k} |\sin(\pi t)| dt=\frac{1}{\pi} \sum_{k=2}^n\frac{1}{k}</math>.

As <math>n</math> is an arbitrary positive integer and <math display="inline">\lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{k=2}^N\frac{1}{k}=+\infty</math>, we obtain a contradiction.

From this example we are able to conclude the following relevant consequences:

* I) Theorem 1 is no longer true for Henstock-Kurzweil integral since <math>g_0</math> is Henstock-Kurzweil integrable and <math>g</math> is not.

* II) Theorem 2 does not hold for McShane integral. Otherwise <math>F'</math> should be McShane integrable as well as <math>g_0</math> and by Theorem 1, as <math>g</math>, which is absurd.

* III) <math>F'</math> is, this way, an example of a Henstock-Kurzweil integrable function which is not McShane integrable. That is, the class of McShane integrable functions is a strict subclass of the Henstock-Kurzweil integrable functions.

== Relationship with Lebesgue Integral ==
The more surprising result of the McShane integral is stated in the following theorem, already announced in the introduction.

=== Theorem 3 ===
Let <math>f:[a,b]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math>. Then

<math>f</math> is McShane integrable <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> <math>f</math> is Lebesgue integrable.

The correspondent integrals coincide.

This fact enables to conclude that with the McShane integral one formulates a kind of unification of the integration theory around Riemann sums, which, after all, constitute the origin of that theory.

So far is not known an immediate proof of such theorem.

In Washek Pfeffer<ref name=":0" /> [Ch. 4] it is stated through the development of the theory of McShane integral, including measure theory, in relationship with already known properties of Lebesgue integral. In Charles Swartz<ref>{{Cite book |last=Swartz |first=Charles |title=Introduction to Gauge Integrals |publisher=World Scientific |year=2001 |isbn=9810242395}}</ref> that same equivalence is proved in Appendix 4.

Furtherly to the book by Russel Gordon<ref name=":2" /> [Ch. 10], on this subject we call the attention of the reader also to the works by Robert McLeod<ref name=":02">{{cite book|date=1980|first=Robert M.|isbn=0-88385-000-1|last=McLeod|location=U. S. A.|publisher=The Mathematical Association of America|title=The Generalized Riemann Integral}}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> [Ch. 8] and Douglas Kurtz together with Charles W. Swartz.<ref name=":1" />

Another perspective of the McShane integral is that it can be looked as new formulation of the Lebesgue integral without using Measure Theory, as alternative to the courses of [[Frigyes Riesz]] and Bela Sz. Nagy<ref>{{cite book|date=1990|first=Béla|isbn=0-486-66289-6|last=Riesz, Frigys e Sz.-Nagy|location=New York|publisher=Dover|title=Functional Analysis}}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> [Ch.II] or [[Serge Lang]]<ref name=":3">{{cite book|date=1983|first=Serge|isbn=978-1-4419-2853-5|last=Lang|location=New York|publisher=Springer-Verlag|title=Undergraduate Analysis}}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref> [Ch.X, §4 Appendix] (see also<ref>{{cite book|date=2012|first=Serge|isbn=978-1-4612-6938-0|last=Lang|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer-Verlag|title=Real and Functional Analysis |edition=3rd. }}<!-- auto-translated by Module:CS1 translator --></ref>).
